procedures.title: Enforce Structured Validation and Early Verification in Software Development Tasks
procedures.knowledge_content: For any software development task, especially those involving complex systems like multiplayer games or multi-agent simulations, follow a two-phase validation strategy: (1) Before code generation, use 'create_solution' with a fully structured, explicit task description that includes all required components (e.g., classes, methods, game mechanics, player abilities, environments, win conditions, and exact naming conventions). This ensures the initial output is grounded in precise requirements. (2) After code generation, always invoke a verification step—such as 'code_review', 'validate_task_completion', 'run_tests', or 'run_unit_tests'—using predefined, quantifiable criteria (e.g., '4-player support', 'Robot.move(dx, dy) signature', 'team objective completion') to validate instruction-following, executability, and core functionality before submission. Never assume partial implementation is sufficient; enforce early detection of missing or mismatched requirements to prevent post-hoc revisions and ensure high-quality, compliant outcomes.

procedures.title: Structured Requirements-First Development with Pre-Submission Validation
procedures.knowledge_content: To ensure successful completion of software development tasks—especially those involving complex, multi-component systems like multiplayer games or multi-agent simulations—follow a two-phase strategy: (1) Always provide explicit, structured, and complete requirements in the initial code generation call (e.g., using JSON keys, class/method signatures, or enumerated lists) to eliminate ambiguity and ensure full feature coverage; avoid vague or partial descriptions. (2) Immediately after code generation, invoke a validation function (e.g., run_tests, validate_code_coverage, code_review, or validate_task_completion) that checks against a predefined checklist of requirements (e.g., player count, environment types, method signatures, win conditions) before any revision or submission. This ensures executability, instruction-following, and quality are verified early, reducing reliance on post-hoc fixes and preventing incomplete implementations from being submitted. Consistently align the solution’s name, structure, and features with the exact task specification to maintain consistency and avoid minor but critical deviations.

procedures.title: Structured Code Development with Pre-Validation and File Integrity Checks
procedures.knowledge_content: When developing software tasks that involve generating and revising code, follow a two-phase workflow: First, always create or write the initial code file using an explicit filename and path (e.g., 'workspace_llmamem/solution.py') to ensure proper file placement and avoid ambiguity. Before performing any review, revision, or advice operations, verify the file's existence in the workspace using a file inspection tool or status check. Then, invoke a structured code review or advice operation with explicit validation prompts that enforce requirement coverage (e.g., 'Verify that team abilities are mapped to puzzle types'). This ensures early detection of missing or inconsistent features, improves executability and consistency, and prevents errors caused by operating on non-existent or misplaced files. Always sequence operations as: create file → confirm existence → invoke review/revision.

procedures.title: Modular Development with Iterative Validation for Multi-Agent Systems
procedures.knowledge_content: When developing multi-agent systems, adopt a structured, iterative approach: first, define formal role specifications with explicit behavioral constraints (e.g., speed, range, abilities) to guide agent design; second, establish a modular code structure by separating components (e.g., Agent, Environment, Rules, Tests) into distinct modules before integration; third, validate each component incrementally using targeted execution or unit tests—such as simulating 2–3 agent interactions or running edge-case scenarios—rather than waiting for final submission; fourth, always verify overall executability with a full system test using realistic inputs (e.g., n_agents=3, specific roles, objectives) before submission. This strategy ensures high executability, maintains code clarity, and catches integration errors early, leading to robust and reliable multi-agent solutions.

procedures.title: Ensure Precondition Validation Before Code Revision
procedures.knowledge_content: Before invoking any code revision or advice-generating function (e.g., give_advice_and_revise), always ensure the following preconditions are met: (1) a valid initial code file (e.g., solution.py) has been created or written using create_file/write_file, (2) the file exists in the workspace and its content has been verified (using file inspection or status checks), (3) any input data (e.g., JSON advice) is syntactically valid (use linters or parsers like json.loads() to validate), and (4) the exact code snippet to be revised matches the current file content, including whitespace and line breaks. Additionally, avoid introducing unnecessary dependencies or features in the initial implementation—start with minimal, core functionality aligned with the task requirements and incrementally enhance based on validation. This strategy prevents revision failures due to missing files, malformed inputs, or mismatched targets, thereby improving consistency, executability, and instruction following across software development tasks.

procedures.title: Modular Development with Pre-Implementation Structure and Incremental Validation
procedures.knowledge_content: Before writing any core implementation code, always initialize a modular project structure using 'create_project_structure' to enforce separation of concerns by creating dedicated directories and files for distinct components (e.g., /src/auth, /src/ui, /src/models, config.json). This prevents monolithic codebases and improves maintainability. Following structure initialization, validate requirements and structure using targeted validation tools ('validate_code_requirements' or 'validate_code_structure') to confirm alignment with technical specifications (e.g., real-time updates, persistence layer, modularity). After each major module is implemented, run incremental validation steps such as 'run_unit_tests' or re-check structure to catch integration issues early, ensuring consistent quality, executability, and instruction adherence throughout development. This strategy minimizes late-stage failures and promotes scalable, testable, and well-organized software.

procedures.title: Structured Code Generation with Verification Pipeline
procedures.knowledge_content: For any software development task requiring the implementation of a complex system (e.g., multiplayer games, multi-agent simulations, or collaborative applications), always follow a two-phase structured approach: (1) Before code generation, invoke 'create_solution' (or equivalent) with a fully detailed, structured specification that explicitly lists all required components — including class definitions, method signatures, data fields, game mechanics, and win conditions — to ensure the generated code is implementable and aligned with requirements. (2) After code generation, always execute a verification step before submission: either 'run_tests', 'run_unit_tests', 'execute_code', or 'code_review' using targeted prompts or test cases that validate core functionality (e.g., entity interactions, team coordination, or objective completion). This verification must be explicit, repeatable, and focused on runtime behavior and requirement coverage, not just syntax. Additionally, ensure filename and task name consistency, and save files to unambiguous paths. This pipeline minimizes incomplete or non-executable outputs and systematically catches logical, structural, and compliance errors early.
